Each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change. Follow the block at the top of the prompt you are answering; an earlier prompt's block no longer applies.

Its spec's Piton source, in ./spec, is only where edits to the spec go.

Read the spec from its compiled reference under .claude/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ./spec to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to .claude/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.

We're working on both the spec and the code, as a chain. This first step changes the spec only, located in ./spec; the code is changed in the next step.

Write the spec so it describes the application as it should be once the prompt is met, and constrains the code. Once you finish, the spec will be built and the same prompt sent to a coding agent, with your reply, to change the code to match it; so end your reply by saying what you changed in the spec and which anchors the code should follow.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.

Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to .suspense/history/1791129571-Prompt_12d373dbb0306780.understanding.md, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.

content.content:
# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user reads, edits, answers, and sends; neither is ever sent by itself.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.
----
Questions asked while another is still running come in at the bottom in the order they were asked, each answered in its own place as its harness goes, so answers can be filling in at once.

#### Suggested Prompts

An answer can hand back a prompt for the user to send, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt`, followed by a space and the mode it is meant for, `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) names them, and holding the prompt's text, as the Ask instructions tell the harness. Such a block is never shown as a code block. It is shown in the answer, where it stands among the reply's markdown, as a prompt card: a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted the mode's colour, with corners rounded 6 pixels, across the answer's full width. Along its top runs a small header, the mode's icon and name in the mode's colour, as "Code prompt", and beneath it the prompt's text as it was written, wrapped, in the body's text colour, not rendered as markdown. Along its bottom, at its right, are two buttons, Copy, with a copy icon, which puts the prompt's text on the clipboard, and "Send to prompt", in the mode's colour, with an arrow icon.
Send to prompt puts the prompt's text in the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s text input and selects the mode's tab, Chain for Code and Spec selected together where the mode is `chain`, giving the input keyboard focus with the cursor at the end of the text. It never sends anything: the user reads, edits, and sends it as any prompt. Where the input already holds text, that text is set aside first as the chat input sets aside a prompt for editing a queued one, and comes back once the prompt from the card is sent or cleared, so nothing typed is lost. What is attached to the prompt being written stays attached. The button reads "Sent to prompt", with a check, for 2 seconds after.
A block whose mode is missing or isn't one of those five is still a prompt card, headed "Prompt", in Ask's colour, and Send to prompt selects Chain, the tab the chat input starts on. While a block is still streaming in, its card is shown with what has come so far and its buttons disabled until the block closes. A block never closed by the end of a finished answer is a card all the same, holding what came. An answer may hold any number of cards, each in its place.

#### Asking Back

An answer can ask the user something back, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, holding the question on its first lines, and then, if the harness offers answers to pick from, one answer per line, each begun with a dash and a space, as a Markdown list item is. Such a block is never shown as a code block. It is shown in the answer, where it stands, as a question card: a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted Ask's colour, with corners rounded 6 pixels, across the answer's full width, holding the question rendered as markdown, and beneath it a button per answer offered, in the order given, each reading that answer.

content.text:
I changed the spec so every Ask question is told to give prompts as cards, and each prompt card gets Send to Code, Send to Chain and Send to Spec buttons. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new sections appear in the refreshed reference.

**The Send buttons send right away.** "Send to Code", "Send to Chain" and "Send to Spec" each send the prompt immediately in that mode, as if you'd typed it on that tab and pressed send. A task queues if its lane is busy. If you'd rather they only fill the chat input for you to send yourself, say so and I'll switch them. The new Edit button does that today.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New `#card-format` section** in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md`
